formations.titre: The Fundamentals of the Christian Faith
formations.accroche: Study Workbook · Questions and answers on the Christian faith. The essential foundations of the faith, based on the clear and infallible teachings of Scripture.
formations.intro:
In a world searching for meaning and truth, the Bible offers timeless and powerful answers. This book aims to guide every reader to discover or rediscover the essential foundations of the Christian faith, based on the clear and infallible teachings of Scripture.

Whether you are a new believer, a Christian seeking to deepen your relationship with God, or simply curious about the central message of Christianity, this book will lead you through the fundamental pillars of the Christian life. Each chapter addresses a key aspect: the plan of salvation, Baptism and the Lord's Supper, the importance of tithes and offerings, as well as the life of the Church and the Christian's witness. These themes, rooted in the Word of God, are not mere theological concepts but transforming truths that shape a new life in Christ.

My desire is that this book will be not only a source of information, but a practical and inspiring tool for living an authentic and radiant faith. Throughout the chapters, you will find biblical explanations, practical examples, and encouragement to put into practice in your daily life.

As you go through these pages, may you be encouraged to walk with God, to grow in your faith, and to live fully the abundant life that Jesus Christ offers to each of His disciples. “I have come that they may have life, and that they may have it more abundantly.” (John 10:10)
objectifs: Know who God is: His attributes, the Trinity
Understand the plan of salvation and conversion
Grasp the meaning of baptism and the Lord's Supper
Live out generosity, the Church, and the new life in Christ

lecons.resume: The one true God, His attributes, the mystery of the Trinity — and the baptism of the Holy Spirit.

sections.p:
We believe in one true God, the Creator of all things: the heavens, the earth, humanity, and the universe. God is Spirit, one in essence yet existing in three distinct persons. His attributes can be divided into two categories:

— Communicable Attributes: characteristics He has shared with us, such as love, will, and intelligence.

— Incommunicable Attributes: attributes belonging to God alone, such as His omnipotence or His omnipresence.

Before going further, let's ask the question that changes everything: why study who God is? Jeremiah 9:23-24 answers powerfully: let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor the rich man in his riches — “but let him who glories glory in this, that he understands and knows Me.” And Jesus goes even further: “This is eternal life, that they may know You, the only true God” (John 17:3). Notice carefully: He doesn't say “that they may know things about You,” but “that they may know You.” Eternal life is not first a destination; it is a relationship.

There is a huge difference between knowing things about God and knowing God. You can read the biography of a famous person and know everything about them without ever having met them; but the day you share a meal with someone, you no longer know them the same way. Look at Moses: this man had seen the burning bush, the ten plagues, the sea split in two, the pillar of fire. And yet, on top of Sinai, what does he ask? “Please, show me Your glory!” (Exodus 33:18). After all he had seen, he still wanted more of God Himself. That is the heart this lesson wants to teach you: never be satisfied with what you know about God, but long for Him.

A word of advice before we continue: don't read this lesson like a course to review. Pause right now and simply tell Him: “Lord, I don't just want to learn things about You — I want to meet You in this lesson.” Every attribute we are about to discover answers a real question in your life: Can I trust Him? Does He see me? Does He change His mind about me?

sections.t: Here Are Some of His Attributes
sections.p:
— Eternal: God was never created. He has always existed and is not limited by time. (Isaiah 40:28; 2 Peter 3:8)

— Sovereign: He rules and reigns over everything and everyone. (Daniel 4:35; Psalms 99:1)

— Almighty: Nothing can defeat God, and nothing is impossible for Him. (Revelation 11:16-17; Jeremiah 32:27; Luke 1:37)

— Omniscient: He knows everything, and nothing can be hidden from His eyes. (Hebrews 4:13; 1 John 3:20)

— Omnipresent: He is everywhere at the same time and fills the whole universe. (Psalms 139:7-8; Jeremiah 23:23-24)

— Immutable: God does not change. He is constant and unchanging. (Hebrews 13:8; James 1:17)

— Holy: God is pure and free from all imperfection or evil. (Revelation 4:8; Isaiah 57:15; 1 Samuel 2:2)

— Love: His very essence is love. He is merciful, good, and patient. (1 John 4:8; Ephesians 2:4; Psalms 34:8; Exodus 34:6)

— Just and perfect: God never makes a mistake and remains faithful in all things. (Zephaniah 3:5; Psalms 7:11; Romans 1:20)

These attributes are not abstract ideas: the Bible shows them to us in action in real lives. Let's take time to look closely at a few of them.

His sovereignty: the story of Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 4). The king of Babylon, the most powerful man in the world, is walking on the roof of his palace, boasting: “Is not this great Babylon, that I have built by my mighty power?” At that very moment, a word falls from heaven: the kingdom is taken from him. For seven times, this proud king lives like a beast of the field, until he lifts his eyes and acknowledges “that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men” (Daniel 4:32). When his reason returns, his first words are worship. Lesson for us: thrones, economies, crises, and our own plans all remain under God's rule. You can go through the darkest news without panicking — no event escapes His hand.

His omniscience: the God who sees me. In Genesis 16, Hagar, a pregnant and mistreated servant, flees into the desert — a woman alone, without status, without a future. It is there that the Angel of the Lord finds her, calls her by name, and speaks to her about her unborn son. Overwhelmed, she gives God this magnificent name: “El Roi,” the God who sees me (Genesis 16:13). Centuries later, Jesus would tell an astonished Nathanael: “Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you” (John 1:48). God saw you before you knew Him. Direct application: since God already knows everything — our doubts, our anger, our shame — prayer can finally become honest. There's no need to put on an act before Him; David prayed without a mask, and that is why the Psalms still touch us today.

His omnipresence: on both sides of running away. Jonah tried to flee “from the presence of the Lord” — he discovered that the ship, the storm, and even the belly of the fish were still before that presence. But omnipresence has a gentler side: in Daniel 3, when the three young men are thrown into the furnace, the king jumps up, astonished: “Did we not cast three men bound…? Look! I see four men walking in the midst of the fire” (Daniel 3:24-25). God had not stayed outside the furnace: He was inside, with them. In a hospital room at three in the morning, in an exam room, in grief — there is no “dead zone” with God, no place where the signal is lost. And in the furnace, He is right beside you.

His immutability: “God is not a man, that He should lie, nor a son of man, that He should repent. Has He said, and will He not do?” (Numbers 23:19). We all know people whose affection changes from day to day; God, however, is exactly the same today as on the day He made His promises. That is what makes faith possible: we build on a rock, not on shifting sand.

His holiness: when Isaiah sees the Lord in the temple, the seraphim themselves cover their faces, crying “Holy, holy, holy!”, and the prophet collapses: “Woe is me, for I am undone! Because I am a man of unclean lips” (Isaiah 6:5). But look at what follows: God's holiness does not destroy Isaiah — a seraph touches his lips with a live coal from the altar, and his sin is taken away. God's holiness is not a distance that crushes: it is a fire that purifies those who draw near.

Finally, His love: God's love is not a changing feeling; it is His very essence — and it has a visible definition: “In this the love of God was manifested toward us, that God has sent His only begotten Son into the world, that we might live through Him” (1 John 4:9). To know whether God loves you, don't look at your circumstances: look at the cross.

The triune nature of God is revealed primarily in the New Testament. Although God manifests Himself in three persons — the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit — He is indivisible. These three persons share the same divine essence and power.

“Then God said, Let Us make man in Our image, according to Our likeness…” (Genesis 1:26)

“For there is one God and one Mediator between God and men, the Man Christ Jesus.” (1 Timothy 2:5)

“When He had been baptized, Jesus came up immediately from the water; and behold, the heavens were opened to Him, and He saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and alighting upon Him. And suddenly a voice came from heaven, saying, This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” (Matthew 3:16-17)

The Trinity is a mystery that goes beyond our human understanding, yet it contains no contradiction. God exists eternally in three distinct persons, perfectly united.

Let's first make one important thing clear: the Trinity was not invented by the Church centuries later — it is woven throughout all of Scripture. From the very first page: “Let Us make man in Our image” (Genesis 1:26) — a mysterious plural at the heart of the one God. And in Jesus' Great Commission, there is a beautiful grammatical detail: baptize “in the NAME of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19) — in the name, singular, not “in the names.” Three persons, one Name, one God.

People have often looked for images to explain the Trinity: water existing as ice, liquid, and steam; the three-leaf clover; the sun with its light and heat. These images may help for a moment, but we need to know their limits. Water is never ice, liquid, and steam at the same time — yet the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit exist together, eternally, in perfect communion. At Jesus' baptism, all three are present at the same moment: the Son in the water, the Spirit descending, the voice of the Father speaking.

Why is this truth so precious, beyond the mystery? For two reasons that touch your life. First: it alone explains that “God is love” (1 John 4:8). Love requires a relationship — you can't love all by yourself. Even before creation, from all eternity, the Father loved the Son in the communion of the Spirit: God did not create the world out of a need to be loved, but out of the overflow of a love that already existed. You weren't born out of a lack, but out of an abundance.

Second: your entire salvation is Trinitarian. Ephesians 1 unfolds it: the Father chose you before the foundation of the world, the Son redeemed you by His blood, the Holy Spirit sealed you for the day of redemption. All three divine persons committed themselves to save you. And that's why Christian prayer has the movement described in Ephesians 2:18: through Jesus, we have access to the Father by one Spirit. When you pray, all of heaven is involved: you speak to the Father, on the basis of the Son's work, carried by the power of the Spirit. The Trinity isn't a theologian's puzzle: it's the house in which you pray.

God the Father is the person of the Trinity who sits enthroned in heaven, sovereign over all creation. He acts as a loving Father toward His children.

“Yet for us there is one God, the Father, of whom are all things, and we for Him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and through whom we live.” (1 Corinthians 8:6)

Let's pause here, because for many people everything hinges on this one word: “Father.” Some of us had fathers who were absent, harsh, unpredictable, or hurtful, and this word stirs up more pain than trust. So we need to answer a crucial question: why is our heavenly Father so different from our earthly fathers?

First, because God didn't become a Father — He has been one from all eternity. A man becomes a father when his child is born, and he learns that role by trial and error, carrying his own wounds. God, however, has always been Father: before creation, He already loved the Son (John 17:24). Fatherhood isn't a role He takes on; it is His very being. Paul says it in a breathtaking phrase: it is from Him that “the whole family in heaven and earth is named” (Ephesians 3:14-15). In other words, God doesn't resemble human fathers — human fathers are called to resemble Him. The best of them are only a pale reflection; the worst are a betrayal of Him. But the original is perfect.

Next, because Scripture takes care to distinguish Him, point by point, from our wounded fathers. Our fathers can abandon us — David writes: “When my father and my mother forsake me, then the Lord will take care of me” (Psalms 27:10). Our fathers can be harsh or fickle — “As a father pities his children, so the Lord pities those who fear Him. For He knows our frame; He remembers that we are dust” (Psalms 103:13-14). Our fathers can give poorly — Jesus Himself makes the argument: “If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask Him!” (Matthew 7:11). Even a mother's love, the strongest we know, is surpassed: “Can a woman forget her nursing child?… Surely they may forget, yet I will not forget you” (Isaiah 49:15).

And when God trains, He doesn't crush: He raises up. In Hosea 11:3-4, God describes Himself as a parent teaching a little one to walk: “I taught Ephraim to walk, taking them by their arms… I drew them with gentle cords, with bands of love.” Picture the scene: a toddler wobbling, two hands reaching out so he won't fall. That's how God taught you to walk in faith — and He hasn't changed His method. Even His discipline is proof of His love: “For whom the Lord loves He chastens, as a father the son in whom he delights” (Hebrews 12:6) — not to punish, but to shape.

Jesus portrayed all of this in the parable of the prodigal son (Luke 15). Take time to look at it in detail. The son demands his share of the inheritance while his father is still alive — in that culture, it meant saying: “You're already dead to me.” The father, incredibly, lets him go. Then comes the famine, the pigs — the ultimate humiliation for a son of Israel — and the speech the son rehearses: “Make me like one of your hired servants.” He hopes for an employee's status; he has lost the very idea of being a son. But the text says: “When he was still a great way off, his father saw him” — so the father had been scanning the horizon, every single day. And he runs — a patriarch never ran; it was beneath his dignity. This one hikes up his robe and runs. Then three gestures, before the son even finishes his confession: the best robe (dignity restored), the ring (the family's authority, like a credit card on his finger), the sandals (slaves went barefoot — sons wear shoes). No probation period, no employee status: a son, fully, immediately.

That's exactly what God does for you in Christ: “As many as received Him, to them He gave the right to become children of God” (John 1:12). And the Spirit you received is not “the spirit of bondage again to fear, but the Spirit of adoption by whom we cry out, Abba, Father!” (Romans 8:15). “Abba” is the word little Aramaic children used — our “Daddy.” A slave doesn't walk into the king's chamber; a little child climbs onto his lap.

How can you apply this if the word “father” hurts you? Here's a concrete path. First, name the wound before God — He already knows, but saying it sets you free. Second, refuse the transfer: every time you catch yourself thinking, “God must be like my father — disappointed, distant, unpredictable,” answer that thought with a verse; read Psalm 103 slowly every morning for a week. Third, pray out loud starting with “Abba, Father” — not as a formula, but because saying the words heals the mouth that could never say them. Fourth, begin the journey of forgiveness toward your earthly father: forgiving isn't excusing or forgetting; it's handing the debt over to God so you no longer carry it yourself. And fifth, let the Church be a family to you: God often heals the image of the father through spiritual fathers and mothers in whom His heart becomes visible.

Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God. He is fully God and fully man, who came to earth to save us.

“Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, being in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but made Himself of no reputation, taking the form of a bondservant, and coming in the likeness of men.” (Philippians 2:6-7)

— Present from the beginning: (John 1:1-3)

— Creator of the universe: (Colossians 1:16)

— Promised from Genesis: (Genesis 3:15)

— His coming prophesied: (Isaiah 53; Micah 5:1; Zechariah 9:9)

— God incarnate: (Isaiah 7:14; John 1:1; Luke 19:10)

— Died for our sins and raised for our justification: (1 Corinthians 15:1-5)

— The only Savior and Mediator: (Acts 4:12; 1 Timothy 2:5)

— Almighty and eternal: (Revelation 22:12-13; Matthew 28:18)

Let's take a close look at these two statements, because the entire Christian faith rests on their union: fully God, fully man.

Fully God: this is not an honorary title. John opens his Gospel the way Genesis opens: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). Jesus does what only God can do: He forgives sins — and the scribes don't miss it: “Who can forgive sins but God alone?” (Mark 2:7); He commands the storm, and it falls silent; He receives worship without ever refusing it, whereas angels and apostles refuse it in alarm. And when Thomas, eight days after the resurrection, touches His wounds and cries out, “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28), Jesus doesn't correct him — He commends him for believing.

Fully man: He was hungry in the wilderness, thirsty at noon by a well (John 4:6-7), He slept from exhaustion in a boat in the middle of a storm, He wept at the tomb of His friend Lazarus (John 11:35), He knew such anguish in Gethsemane that His sweat became like great drops of blood. He “was in all points tempted as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15). His humanity wasn't a disguise: it was real flesh, real fatigue, real tears.

Why must He absolutely be both? Follow the reasoning closely, because its logic is brilliantly clear. The debt of sin is a human debt: man sinned, so man must pay. But no man can: each one is already bankrupt from his own debt. Only God has the means to pay — but God owed nothing. So it took someone who had to pay as a man and who could pay as God: Jesus, and Him alone. That's why “there is one Mediator between God and men, the Man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). Imagine a mediator tasked with reconciling two peoples who don't speak the same language: he must speak both perfectly. Jesus places one hand on God and one hand on us, and He brings us together.

And consider how far down He agreed to come. Philippians 2:6-7 describes this willing descent: though He was in the form of God, He didn't cling to His rank — He emptied Himself. From the glory of heaven to a stable's manger; from the worship of angels to the spit of a judgment hall; from the throne to the cross. No one took His life from Him: He laid it down (John 10:18). When you wonder what you're worth in God's eyes, look at the price He agreed to pay.

Here's a very practical consequence for your prayer life: because your advocate with the Father knows hardship from the inside, you can “come boldly to the throne of grace, that you may obtain mercy and find grace to help in time of need” (Hebrews 4:16). When you pray in your suffering, you're not talking to someone watching from a distance — you're talking to someone who has been there.

The Holy Spirit is the Spirit of God. He is a divine person, not merely a force or an influence. He is the One who convicts hearts, teaches believers, and transforms them into the image of Christ. He is the person of God who dwells within us.

— He speaks (Hebrews 3:7),

— He leads (Galatians 5:18),

— He gives gifts (1 Corinthians 12:11),

— He can be grieved (Ephesians 4:30).

“But the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in My name, He will teach you all things, and bring to your remembrance all things that I said to you.” (John 14:26)

“You shall receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you; and you shall be witnesses to Me…” (Acts 1:8)

His role:

1. To convict of sin (John 16:8-11).

2. To dwell in the believer: our body becomes the temple of God (1 Corinthians 6:19).

3. To produce the character of Christ: the Spirit sanctifies us and makes us like the Father (Matthew 5:48).

Let's hold firmly to this truth: the Holy Spirit is someone, not something. He is not an impersonal energy or a “force” like in the movies. Here is the proof from Scripture: a force doesn't speak — yet “the Spirit said to Philip, ‘Go near and overtake this chariot’” (Acts 8:29); a force doesn't make decisions — yet He is the one who distributes gifts “to each one individually as He wills” (1 Corinthians 12:11); a force cannot be grieved — yet Paul writes, “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God” (Ephesians 4:30); you can't lie to a force — yet Peter says to Ananias, “Why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit?… You have not lied to men but to God” (Acts 5:3-4). Notice, by the way, what that last sentence reveals: lying to the Holy Spirit is lying to God — the Spirit is fully God.

Jesus calls Him the “Helper” — in Greek paraklētos, literally “the one called alongside”: an advocate who stands beside you in court, a friend who walks next to you on a difficult road. And on the eve of His death, Jesus says something astonishing: “It is to your advantage that I go away; for if I do not go away, the Helper will not come to you” (John 16:7). To your advantage! Jesus in the flesh was with His disciples; by the Spirit, He is in each of them, everywhere, always. You don't have a diminished version of God's presence: you have the presence promised as an advantage.

Watch Him at work in the book of Acts to understand how He still works today: He tells Philip to catch up with a chariot on a desert road — and an Ethiopian official encounters the Gospel (Acts 8); He tells the church in Antioch, “Now separate to Me Barnabas and Saul” — and the worldwide mission begins (Acts 13:2); He prevents Paul from going into Asia and sends him to Macedonia — and the Gospel enters Europe (Acts 16:6-10). The Spirit speaks, directs, and sends. The Christian life is not a rulebook to follow; it is a Person to follow.

In practical terms, this changes your everyday life: a Christian is never left to his own strength. It is the Spirit who reminds you of the Word at the right moment, who gives you the words when it's time to testify, who gently corrects you when you take a wrong path, and who prays within you when you no longer know how to pray (Romans 8:26). Learning the Christian life means learning to be sensitive to His voice: begin each day by simply telling Him, “Holy Spirit, You are welcome — lead me today,” obey quickly the holy promptings He gives you (that person to call, that forgiveness to ask for, that verse that keeps coming back), and be careful not to grieve Him by what you watch, say, or feed on. “Do not quench the Spirit” (1 Thessalonians 5:19): you put out a fire by no longer feeding it — you keep it burning by adding wood every day.

sections.t: The Baptism of the Holy Spirit
sections.p:
The baptism of the Holy Spirit is a powerful spiritual experience in which a person is filled with the Holy Spirit, receiving His presence, His power, and His working all at once in order to accomplish God's will. It is distinct from water baptism, which symbolizes repentance and commitment to Christ.

In Acts 1:4-5, Jesus tells His disciples: “Do not depart from Jerusalem, but wait for the Promise of the Father, which you have heard from Me; for John truly baptized with water, but you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.”

This passage shows that the baptism of the Holy Spirit is an event distinct from water baptism and that it is a promise from God to His children.

To understand this well, let's distinguish two realities. At conversion, the Holy Spirit comes to dwell in you: every born-again Christian has the Spirit — “if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not His” (Romans 8:9). The baptism of the Holy Spirit, on the other hand, is an immersion in His power: like a glass already full that begins to overflow onto everything around it. The water is the same; the measure changes.

The book of Acts shows this distinction in action, not just in theory. At Pentecost (Acts 2), disciples who already believed are filled and overflow into the streets of Jerusalem. In Samaria (Acts 8), people believed and were baptized in water — then Peter and John come to pray for them to receive the Holy Spirit: two distinct moments. At Cornelius's house (Acts 10), the Spirit falls during the preaching, even before water baptism — God is not bound to a fixed order. And in Ephesus (Acts 19), Paul meets sincere disciples and asks them this surprising question: “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” The question itself proves that one can be a believer and not yet have had this experience — otherwise it would make no sense.

This is not a reward for super-Christians, but equipment for all of God's children. The promise of Acts 2:39 is explicit: it is “to you and to your children, and to all who are afar off” — in other words, to you.

sections.t: The Manifestation of the Baptism of the Holy Spirit
sections.p:
The day of Pentecost was the fulfillment of this promise. Here is what is written:

“When the Day of Pentecost had fully come, they were all with one accord in one place. And suddenly there came a sound from heaven, as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting. Then there appeared to them divided tongues, as of fire, and one sat upon each of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance.” (Acts 2:1-4)

This experience is characterized by:

— Spiritual power: “You shall receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you” (Acts 1:8).

— Outward signs such as speaking in tongues.

— Inner transformation and boldness to testify of Christ: the disciples, who were fearful before Pentecost, became courageous witnesses afterward.

sections.t: Why Is the Baptism of the Holy Spirit Important?
sections.p:
a) To receive God's power. Jesus said, “You shall receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you; and you shall be witnesses to Me” (Acts 1:8). The baptism of the Holy Spirit gives supernatural strength to live for Christ, overcome spiritual challenges, and proclaim the Gospel with confidence.

b) To be filled with the Spirit of God. Paul teaches that we must be continually filled with the Holy Spirit: “Do not be drunk with wine, in which is dissipation; but be filled with the Spirit.” (Ephesians 5:18) The baptism of the Holy Spirit marks the beginning of a Spirit-filled life, in which the believer is guided and transformed by God.

c) To receive spiritual gifts. In 1 Corinthians 12, Paul explains that the Holy Spirit gives spiritual gifts for building up the Church, such as prophecy, speaking in tongues, wisdom, faith, miracles, and more. These gifts are often experienced after the believer's conversion.

The most striking example is Peter himself. Before Pentecost, this man who had walked with Jesus for three years — who had seen the miracles, heard all the teachings, and confessed “You are the Christ” — denies his Master three times, before a mere servant girl, around a fire. Three years of the best training in the world, given by the best Teacher in the world, were not enough to overcome his fear. A few weeks later, the same Peter stands up before thousands of people in Jerusalem, in the very city where his Master had just been executed, and preaches with such authority that three thousand people are saved that very day. What changed between those two scenes? Just one thing: Pentecost. It wasn't training that transformed Peter; it was power.

And Peter is not an isolated case: Stephen, a simple servant waiting on tables, “full of grace and power,” stands up to the scholars and forgives his executioners as he dies (Acts 6-7); Paul would say that his preaching did not rest “on persuasive words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power” (1 Corinthians 2:4). The biblical pattern is consistent: the Spirit's power is not a luxury for conference speakers; it is the normal equipment of a witness.

That is why this experience concerns you: we all have our own “servant girl's courtyard,” those moments when fear shuts our mouths — in front of a coworker, at a family dinner, when faced with an opportunity to pray for someone. The baptism of the Holy Spirit doesn't make you perfect, but it makes you a witness. And the gifts He distributes (1 Corinthians 12) are not first-century museum pieces: “Pursue love, and desire spiritual gifts” (1 Corinthians 14:1) is a command still in force — a word of encouragement given at the right time, a prayer for someone who is sick, a word of knowledge that shows God sees: so many ways God concretely touches lives today, in order and in love (1 Corinthians 13 and 14).

sections.t: How Do You Receive the Baptism of the Holy Spirit?
sections.p:
The Bible teaches that the baptism of the Holy Spirit is a gift God gives to those who ask in faith. Here are some biblical steps:

a) Believe in Jesus Christ as Lord and Savior. The baptism of the Holy Spirit is for those who are already born again. Peter says, “Repent, and let every one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins; and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. For the promise is to you and to your children, and to all who are afar off, as many as the Lord our God will call.” (Acts 2:38-39)

b) Ask in faith. Jesus taught that the heavenly Father gladly gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask: “If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him!” (Luke 11:13)

c) Persevere in prayer. In Acts 1:14, the disciples continued steadfastly in prayer before receiving the Holy Spirit. Persistent prayer is a key to receiving this blessing.

d) Submit your life to God. The Holy Spirit works in a life surrendered to God. The more open we are to Him and sensitive to His voice, the more He fills our lives.

A Christian needs the “power” of the Holy Spirit to function fully in the Christian life. The baptism of the Holy Spirit is like plugging a phone into a power source: it fills, transforms, and gives the ability to do what is impossible in our own strength.

In practical terms, how does it happen? There is no magic formula or technique: there is a Father who loves to give. But the Bible and the experience of the Church outline a simple path, and here it is.

Prepare your heart. The Spirit is holy: He fills vessels that allow themselves to be cleansed. Take a moment to confess what needs confessing, forgive whoever you need to forgive, and give up what needs to be let go. Not to earn the gift — a gift can't be earned — but to receive it with open hands.

Ask with confidence, and surround yourself with others. In the life of the Church, this often happens simply: at the end of a service or during a prayer night, ask the elders or your pastor to pray for you, often with the laying on of hands, as in Samaria (Acts 8:17). There is nothing magical about the hands — but there is something biblical about a Church that prays for its members.

Receive, and step out. On the day of Pentecost, the text says they “began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts 2:4): notice both halves — the Spirit gives, and they speak. God doesn't force your mouth; He invites a trusting cooperation. Many experience this moment in worship: as they keep adoring Him, their own words run out, and the Spirit gives a new language to carry on. If it doesn't come right away, don't tense up: sometimes God answers immediately; sometimes He teaches us perseverance, like the disciples who prayed for ten days before Pentecost.

Then, keep the fire burning. The baptism of the Holy Spirit is not a trophy to set on a shelf; it is an entry door: “But you, beloved, building yourselves up on your most holy faith, praying in the Holy Spirit” (Jude 20). Pray regularly in tongues if you have received this gift, stay in worship, ask to be filled again — the verb in Ephesians 5:18 is a continuous present: “be continually filled with the Spirit.”

Two final pieces of advice: come with an open heart, not a tense one — you don't earn a gift, you receive it. And don't compare your experience with other people's: God is a Father, not a factory; He knows each of His children and leads each one personally.

God, in all His majesty and glory, reveals Himself as one being in essence, yet manifested in three persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Creator of the entire universe, He is at once eternal, all-powerful, all-knowing, just, and infinitely loving. Each of God's attributes reveals a facet of His perfection and greatness, inviting believers into sincere and profound worship.

The Trinity, though a mystery beyond our full understanding, bears witness to the perfect unity and harmony within God. The Father loves, the Son saves, and the Holy Spirit transforms and sanctifies. Together, they work in the lives of believers to lead them into a personal, living relationship with their Creator.

As we discover who God is, we are called to worship Him, to serve Him, and to live according to His will. This infinite and unsearchable God earnestly desires fellowship with each of His children, inviting them to live in holiness, faith, and love.

“For You are great, and do wondrous things; You alone are God.” (Psalms 86:10)

The baptism of the Holy Spirit is a biblical and essential experience in the Christian life. It is a promise God gives to all who believe in Jesus Christ and who long to receive His power to live a life filled with His presence and to be effective witnesses in this world. If you have not yet experienced it, know that God is ready to give it to you. Seek Him in prayer, open your heart to Him, and wait on Him in faith. God is faithful!

quiz.q: How many Gods are there, and in how many persons does He reveal Himself?
choix: One God in one single person
Two gods: the Father and the Son
quiz.explication: God is one in essence, manifested in three perfectly united persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit (Genesis 1:26; Matthew 3:16-17).

quiz.q: What does the attribute “immutable” mean?
quiz.explication: God is constant and unchanging: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever” (Hebrews 13:8).

quiz.q: The Holy Spirit is…
quiz.explication: He speaks, leads, gives gifts, and can be grieved (Ephesians 4:30) — everything of a person, nothing of an energy.

quiz.q: What is the baptism of the Holy Spirit?
choix: Being filled with the presence and power of the Spirit
quiz.explication: It is an experience distinct from water baptism, promised by Jesus (Acts 1:4-5) and fulfilled at Pentecost (Acts 2:1-4).

quiz.q: How do you receive the baptism of the Holy Spirit?
choix: By earning it through good works
By asking for it with faith and perseverance
quiz.explication: “Your heavenly Father will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him” (Luke 11:13) — ask in faith, persevere in prayer, submit to God.

quiz.q: What is the difference between God's “communicable” and “incommunicable” attributes?
choix: The first are found in the Old Testament, the second in the New
The first are shared with us (love, intelligence), the second belong to God alone (omnipresence)
The first concern the Father, the second the Holy Spirit
There is no difference between the two
quiz.explication: Communicable attributes are characteristics God has shared with us, such as love and intelligence; incommunicable ones, such as omnipotence or omnipresence, belong to Him alone.

quiz.q: What does the attribute “omnipresent” mean?
choix: God is everywhere at the same time
quiz.explication: Omnipresent means that God is everywhere at the same time and fills the whole universe (Psalms 139:7-8): there is no place where you are alone.

quiz.q: At Jesus' baptism (Matthew 3:16-17), how are the three persons of the Trinity present together?
choix: They appear one after another, never at the same time
The Son in the water, the Spirit descending like a dove, the voice of the Father speaking
Only the Father and the Son are mentioned
The scene is a symbolic vision with no reality
quiz.explication: This scene shows the three divine persons present at the same moment — something images like water (ice, liquid, steam) cannot capture.

quiz.q: In the parable of the prodigal son (Luke 15:20), what does the father do when he sees his son returning?
choix: He waits for the son to apologize before welcoming him
He takes him in as a servant, on probation
He runs to meet him, moved with compassion, and embraces him
He demands back the squandered inheritance
quiz.explication: “When he was still a great way off, his father saw him and had compassion, and ran and fell on his neck.” That is the Father's heart for each of His children.

quiz.q: What transformed Peter between his denial and his bold preaching before thousands of people?
choix: The power of the Holy Spirit received at Pentecost
quiz.explication: Between the two scenes, only one thing changed: Pentecost. It wasn't training that transformed Peter — it was the power of the Holy Spirit.

sections.p:
In the beginning, God created man good, in His image, like all of creation, which He declared “very good” (Genesis 1:31). Man was destined for perfect fellowship with his Creator, enjoying absolute happiness and balance, in harmony with himself, with nature, and with God. But man's disobedience brought a dramatic rupture: the “fall.” This disobedience destroyed the harmony between God and humanity.

Because of sin, man was separated from God and had to bear the consequences:

— Physical death: he became mortal.

— Spiritual death: he was cut off from fellowship with God.

— Inner corruption: sin infected his heart and his relationships.

— Deterioration of nature: the world became marked by destruction and disorder.

Thus, man cannot reach God through his own efforts (Isaiah 64:5; Romans 3:10-20). But in His infinite love, God took the initiative to reconcile humanity to Himself.

“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” (Romans 3:23)

“For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.” (Romans 6:23)

The Greek word translated “sin,” hamartia, comes from the vocabulary of archery: it means “to miss the mark.” That corrects a common misconception. Sin is not first of all a list of serious acts reserved for hardened criminals: it is a missed target — life as God dreamed it for us, which we all fall short of.

Imagine a long-jump contest at the edge of a canyon three miles wide. An Olympic champion will jump twenty-eight feet; a child will jump three feet. The difference between them is real, but compared to three miles, it no longer matters. No one reaches the other side. That is exactly what Romans 3:23 says: all have sinned and “fall short of the glory of God.” Compared to one another, we are more or less “good”; compared to God's holiness, we all need a bridge — not a better running start.

And look how honestly the Bible describes this diagnosis in real lives. David, the man “after God's own heart,” commits adultery and then has an innocent man killed to cover it up — and when the prophet Nathan comes to confront him with the parable of the stolen lamb, David is outraged at the rich thief… until Nathan tells him, “You are the man!” (2 Samuel 12:7). That is the nature of sin: we see it perfectly in others, and it blinds us to ourselves. That is why God's first grace is to open our eyes.

One last word on the “fall”: it explains the world as you see it. Why so much beauty AND so much violence? Because the world is a magnificent work… that has been damaged. Like a bombed-out cathedral: the ruins still bear witness to the architect's splendor, and at the same time to the disaster. The Bible is the only story that accounts for both at once — and that announces restoration.

Salvation does not rest on human effort, but on God's love and work. God offered His own Son, Jesus Christ, as a sacrifice for sin.

“For God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son, that whoever believes in Him should not perish but have everlasting life.” (John 3:16)

Jesus came to bear the sins of the world. John the Baptist declared, “Behold! The Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29). Jesus, perfectly sinless, was the only one able to satisfy divine justice.

“For He made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in Him.” (2 Corinthians 5:21)

At the cross, Jesus displayed both the love and the justice of God (Romans 3:25-26). His death and resurrection are at the heart of the Gospel. Without them, there would be neither salvation nor good news.

“Nor is there salvation in any other, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved.” (Acts 4:12)

To grasp what happened at the cross, picture this courtroom scene: a judge sees a guilty man brought before him whose debt is crushing. Because he is just, the judge cannot pretend nothing happened: the wrong must be paid for. But at the end of the hearing, the judge stands up, takes off his robe, steps down from the bench… and pays the debt himself. Justice is satisfied, and the guilty man goes free. That is the cross: God did not turn a blind eye to evil — He paid its price Himself, in person.

This is what the Bible calls substitution, and it had been foretold centuries in advance. Isaiah 53, written seven hundred years before the cross, describes the Servant with stunning precision: “He was wounded for our transgressions, He was bruised for our iniquities; the chastisement for our peace was upon Him” (Isaiah 53:5). Notice the pronouns: our sins, upon Him. The whole Gospel is contained in that exchange. And already in Eden, God had sketched it out: to cover Adam and Eve in their shame, He made tunics of skin (Genesis 3:21) — an animal had to die so that man could be covered. The first shadow of the cross, on the third page of the Bible.

One detail of the account deserves a closer look: at the moment Jesus dies, “the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom” (Matthew 27:51). That thick veil separated the Most Holy Place — the presence of God — from the rest of the world; only one person passed through it, only once a year. Torn from top to bottom: not by human hands from below, but by God from above. The message is clear: access is open. You no longer need a priest, a ritual, or merit to draw near — the way is open, at the cost of Jesus' torn body.

And never forget the second half of the Gospel: the resurrection. If Jesus had stayed in the tomb, His death would have been a beautiful but powerless gesture — “if Christ is not risen, your faith is futile” (1 Corinthians 15:17). But the tomb is empty: it is the receipt for the payment, the proof that the sacrifice was accepted, and the guarantee of our own resurrection. We do not follow an admirable martyr: we follow the Living One.

Salvation is a free gift from God, but each person must receive it through faith and repentance. Conversion is a radical change by which a person abandons sin and turns to God.

“For I have no pleasure in the death of one who dies,” says the Lord God. “Therefore turn and live!” (Ezekiel 18:32)

The Bible describes two essential elements of conversion (Acts 20:20-21):

— Repentance: sincerely acknowledging your sins, grieving over them, and turning away from them. It shows up as a visible abandonment of the practices that displease God (Luke 3:8; Acts 26:20).

— Faith: trusting God and the sacrifice of Jesus for the forgiveness of our sins. It does not rest on human works but on divine grace (Romans 10:9).

“For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God.” (Ephesians 2:8-9)

The Greek word for “repentance,” metanoia, means a change of mind that leads to a change of direction. The simplest picture is a U-turn: you’re driving down a road, you realize you’re headed the wrong way, and regret isn’t enough—as long as you keep driving, you keep getting farther away. To repent is to turn around.

The Bible shows us the difference between a true and a false U-turn through two men on the same night. Judas betrayed Jesus; Peter denied Him. Both felt heartbreaking regret. But Judas locked himself in his remorse until he reached despair, while Peter wept bitterly… and then came back to Jesus, who restored him by the lake (John 21). Paul sums it up: “Godly sorrow produces repentance leading to salvation, but worldly sorrow produces death” (2 Corinthians 7:10). True repentance doesn’t end with you and your shame—it ends in the arms of God.

Zacchaeus is the most joyful example (Luke 19). This chief tax collector, who had grown rich at his people’s expense and was despised by everyone, climbs a sycamore tree to catch a glimpse of Jesus—and Jesus stops under the tree, calls him by name, and invites Himself to his house. And Zacchaeus’s repentance doesn’t stay a feeling: “I give half of my goods to the poor; and if I have taken anything from anyone by false accusation, I restore fourfold.” His ledger is converted along with his heart. True repentance can be seen—in actions, relationships, finances, habits.

Finally, notice what conversion is not: a performance to earn God’s love. The order of the Gospel is crucial. Jesus invites Himself to Zacchaeus’s house BEFORE Zacchaeus changes—and it is that undeserved grace that changes him. God doesn’t say, “Change, and I’ll love you”; He says, “I love you—come, and you will be changed.” Repentance isn’t the price of admission; it’s the response of a heart that has been touched.

When someone turns to God, profound transformations take place:

— A new creation: “If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new.” (2 Corinthians 5:17)

— The indwelling of the Holy Spirit: God places His life within him by His Spirit. “He who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through His Spirit who dwells in you.” (Romans 8:11)

— Adoption as a child of God: “Behold what manner of love the Father has bestowed on us, that we should be called children of God!” (1 John 3:1)

— Sanctification: the Christian life is called to reflect God’s holiness. This process of transformation lasts a lifetime.

Let’s be clear about what conversion is not: a simple upgrade of the old self. God doesn’t repaint the front of a house in ruins; He rebuilds. The Bible doesn’t say, “If anyone is in Christ, he becomes a little better,” but “he is a new creation” (2 Corinthians 5:17). It’s a heart transplant, not a coat of paint—exactly what God had promised through Ezekiel: “I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you; I will take the heart of stone out of your flesh and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 36:26).

Jesus used another, even more radical image in His nighttime conversation with Nicodemus (John 3). Nicodemus was no beginner: a teacher of the law, a religious leader, beyond reproach. Yet it is to him that Jesus says, “You must be born again.” Not “you need to try a bit harder,” not “work on this area”—be born. You don’t improve your way into birth; you receive it. If the most serious religion in the world wasn’t enough for Nicodemus, our good resolutions won’t be enough for us either.

This sheds light on an experience many new believers know: changing tastes, habits that lose their appeal, a new hunger for the Word and prayer, a surprising love for people you would never have spent time with. Not that everything becomes easy overnight—sanctification lasts a lifetime, and Romans 7 honestly describes our struggles—but the deep direction of the heart has changed. A baby doesn’t become an adult in a day; yet it is fully alive from birth, and its growth is certain because life is within it.

A practical application if you’ve just come to faith: don’t measure your new birth by the emotions of the day, but by the signs of life God lists—an appetite for His Word, the reflex of prayer, quick sorrow when you sin and the desire to come back, love for your brothers and sisters (1 John lists them). And if one day you doubt that you’re a child of God, don’t look within yourself: look at the promise—“He who believes in the Son has everlasting life” (John 3:36). Your assurance doesn’t rest on the strength of your faith, but on the faithfulness of the One you believe in.

Faith is complete trust in God and in His promises. It means leaning on Him, even for things that are unseen or beyond understanding.

“Now faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen.” (Hebrews 11:1)

Faith opens the door to divine intervention and enables the believer to live beyond human limitations.

“If you have faith as a mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move; and nothing will be impossible for you.” (Matthew 17:20)

What is faith, in practical terms? Take a very simple picture: a chair. You can examine a chair, find it sturdy, and state with conviction that it can hold you—but as long as you stay standing, that’s not faith yet; it’s an opinion. Faith is sitting down. It’s the moment you rest your weight on it.

Many people “believe in God” the way you’d have an opinion about a chair: from a distance, without ever sitting down. James goes so far as to say that “even the demons believe—and tremble!” (James 2:19)—accurate information saves no one. Biblical faith rests the full weight of your life—your forgiveness, your future, your eternity—on Jesus.

Look at Abraham, whom the Bible calls “the father of all those who believe.” God promises him a son when he is a hundred years old and Sarah is past childbearing age. Romans 4 describes his faith with beautiful honesty: “He did not waver at the promise of God through unbelief, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God, and being fully convinced that what He had promised He was also able to perform” (Romans 4:20-21). Notice what his faith rests on: not on his own abilities—he knew they were as good as dead—but on the faithfulness of the One who promised. Faith isn’t optimism (“everything will be fine”) or self-suggestion (“I believe really hard”): it’s trust placed in a promise and in the character of God.

That’s why a mustard seed is enough: the power of faith doesn’t come from its intensity, but from its object. Huge faith placed on ice that’s too thin ends up in freezing water; small faith placed on a solid bridge crosses the river. When your faith feels weak, don’t stare at it—gaze at your God. You don’t strengthen your faith by focusing on it, but by looking to the One who deserves it: “Faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of Christ” (Romans 10:17). Feed your faith on the Word, and it will grow without you even noticing.

1. Eternal life: through Jesus Christ, the believer receives eternal life (John 3:16).

2. The Holy Spirit: God gives His Spirit to those who believe (Galatians 3:2).

3. Justification: a person is declared righteous before God (Galatians 2:16).

4. Nearness to God: by faith, the believer draws near to God with confidence (Hebrews 10:22).

5. Victory over sin: “For whatever is born of God overcomes the world. And this is the victory that has overcome the world—our faith.” (1 John 5:4)

“So that the tested genuineness of your faith, more precious than gold that perishes, may be found to result in praise, glory, and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ.” (1 Peter 1:6-7)

God uses trials to purify and strengthen the faith of His children. They are opportunities for spiritual growth, allowing the believer to rely more and more on God’s grace.

Why does God allow trials? The image in 1 Peter is that of a goldsmith: gold is refined by fire, which brings impurities to the surface—and it’s said that the goldsmith knows the gold is pure when he can see himself in it like a mirror. In the same way, trials reveal what is truly in our hearts and allow God to refine it… until the image of Christ is reflected there. A muscle only grows stronger under resistance; a faith that has never been tested doesn’t yet know how strong it is.

The story of Joseph is the great school of this mystery (Genesis 37–50). Sold by his own brothers, a slave in Egypt, falsely accused, forgotten in prison for years—everything seemed to contradict the promises God had given him in dreams. But trace the thread: the pit leads to Egypt, Potiphar’s house leads to prison, prison leads to the palace—and the palace will save entire nations from famine, including the guilty brothers. At the end of the road, Joseph can tell them without bitterness: “You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20). God had not abandoned the dark years: He was at work in them.

But be careful not to mix everything up: God is not the author of evil, and the Bible never asks us to call evil “good.” It promises something else, something more solid: that nothing—not betrayal, not injustice, not illness—is beyond His power to turn it for the good of those who love Him (Romans 8:28). In His hands, what was meant to destroy you becomes what shapes you.

In practical terms, in the midst of a trial: don’t first ask “why?”—a question whose answer often comes years later, as it did for Joseph—but “with whom?” (He is in the furnace with you) and “for what?” (what does He want to form in me?). Keep praying even when you don’t feel anything, stay in fellowship with other believers instead of isolating yourself, and keep a journal of God’s faithfulness: in the next battle, you’ll remember that He has never failed.

The plan of salvation is a magnificent work of God’s grace and love—He gave His only Son, Jesus Christ, to reconcile humanity to Himself. All people are sinners, unable to reach God through their own efforts, but God, in His immense love, has provided a way of salvation through the cross and resurrection of Jesus.

Repentance and faith are the keys to receiving this salvation. Repentance means sincerely turning away from sin, while faith places complete trust in Jesus and His sacrifice for the forgiveness of our sins. Through this step, a person becomes a new creation, receives the Holy Spirit, and enters into an intimate relationship with God as His child.

This salvation is not the fruit of human works, but a free gift offered by God’s grace. Faith opens the door to a transformed life, to justification, to victory over sin, and to an eternal hope. Even through trials, faith is strengthened, enabling the believer to grow spiritually and to live fully in the light of Christ.

“For God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son, that whoever believes in Him should not perish but have everlasting life.” (John 3:16)

I commit to acknowledging my condition as a sinner and to living in a constant attitude of repentance, abandoning everything that displeases God.

I commit to placing my faith entirely in Jesus Christ, acknowledging Him as my Savior and Lord, and trusting Him for the forgiveness of my sins and the salvation of my soul.

I commit to living as a new creation, allowing the Holy Spirit to transform my life, my thoughts, and my actions.

I commit to cultivating intimate fellowship with God through prayer, reading the Bible, and obeying His commandments.

Finally, I commit to bearing witness to God’s love and grace through my life and my words, sharing the good news of salvation with those around me, so that others may also know the joy of a restored relationship with their Creator.
