Feed your faith: read the Bible every day, meditate on its promises, and hand your worries over to God (Romans 10:17)
Live as a new creation: let the Holy Spirit transform your life and pursue the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22-23)
Stay connected to God: pray regularly and meditate on a Bible passage daily to grow in your relationship with Him
Share your faith: simply testify to what God has done in your life and invite others to discover Jesus
Obey God in the little things: honor Him faithfully in your daily decisions, even the simplest ones
Persevere through trials: stay faithful by leaning on God's grace and the support of your Christian community

quiz.q: Why can't people save themselves?
choix: Because they don't try hard enough
Because all have sinned and are separated from God
Because God doesn't want them to
quiz.explication: “All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23) — no human effort can bridge that separation.

quiz.q: What is the means of salvation?
choix: The death and resurrection of Jesus
quiz.explication: God offered His own Son as a sacrifice for sin (John 3:16; 2 Corinthians 5:21). Without the cross and the resurrection, there is no Gospel.

quiz.q: What are the two essential elements of conversion?
quiz.explication: Sincerely turning away from sin (repentance) and placing complete trust in Jesus (faith) — Acts 20:21.

quiz.q: What does a person who turns to Christ become?
choix: A new creation, a child of God
quiz.explication: “If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation” (2 Corinthians 5:17) — adopted as a child of God (1 John 3:1).

quiz.q: Based on Ephesians 2:8-9, salvation comes…
choix: From our efforts and grace in equal parts
quiz.explication: “For by grace you have been saved through faith… not of works, lest anyone should boast.”

quiz.q: What does the Greek word hamartia, translated as “sin,” mean?
quiz.explication: Hamartia comes from archery vocabulary: missing the mark — the life God intended, which we all miss (Romans 3:23).

quiz.q: What were the consequences of the fall for mankind?
choix: Physical and spiritual death, inner corruption, and the deterioration of creation
The loss of the memory of Eden
None: God forgave everything right away
quiz.explication: Disobedience affected everything: man became mortal, cut off from fellowship with God, inwardly corrupted, in a world marked by disorder.

quiz.q: What does the word “repentance” (metanoia) mean?
choix: A change of mind that leads to turning around
quiz.explication: Regret isn't enough: as long as you keep driving in the wrong direction, you keep moving away. To repent is to turn around — like Zacchaeus, whose life changed in action.

quiz.q: In the illustration of the chair, what represents faith?
choix: Examining the chair and finding it sturdy
Declaring with conviction that it can hold us
Sitting down: resting your whole weight on it
quiz.explication: Believing a chair is sturdy is just an opinion. Faith is sitting down — resting the weight of your life on Jesus.

quiz.q: Based on Hebrews 11:1, what is faith?
choix: The assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen
A reward reserved for the most faithful
quiz.explication: Faith is not an emotion but trust placed in God and His promises — and its strength comes from its object, not its intensity.

lecons.resume: Buried and raised with Christ: the public testimony of your new life.

sections.p:
“John came baptizing in the wilderness and preaching a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins.” (Mark 1:4)

Baptism is a visible representation of the new birth. It is a commitment the new believer makes with God, a public testimony of his faith. Following the biblical example, he is immersed in water, symbolizing an inner transformation.

“Do you not know that as many of us as were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into His death? Therefore we were buried with Him through baptism into death, that just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life.” (Romans 6:3-11)

During baptism, the disciple is fully immersed in the water before coming back up. This act symbolizes death and resurrection: a passage from death to life. By identifying with Christ's death through immersion, the one being baptized testifies to his desire to put his old nature to death in order to live a new life in Christ.

“…buried with Him in baptism, in which you also were raised with Him through faith in the working of God, who raised Him from the dead.” (Colossians 2:12)

Also read: 1 Peter 3:18-22; Galatians 3:27; Ephesians 4:5; Titus 3:5; Hebrews 6:2.

To really grasp the nature of baptism, think of a wedding ring. The ring doesn't create the couple's love; you can be married without a ring, and wear a ring without being married. But on the wedding day, before witnesses, the ring slipped onto the finger publicly proclaims: “I am hers, I am his, forever.” Baptism plays that role: it doesn't produce salvation, it proclaims it. It is the public declaration of an inner reality already born — a heart that now belongs to Christ.

But the symbol goes further than proclamation: it tells the story of a death and a resurrection. Romans 6 is explicit — going down into the water is being “buried with Christ”; coming up out of it is “walking in newness of life.” The water is both a tomb and a womb: the old self is buried there, and you come out newborn. The early Christians lived this so concretely that in many ancient churches, the person being baptized entered the water by steps on the west — the side of the setting sun, of the old life — and came out by steps on the east, toward the rising sun.

And like the ring, baptism commits you. After the ceremony, you live differently: you bear a name, a faithfulness, a visible belonging. The baptized person comes out of the water with this awareness: my life is no longer my own, and everyone knows it. It's a grace, not a burden — just as it's easier to keep a commitment the whole world knows about.

We baptize new believers in obedience to a clear command from Jesus. It isn't just an option, but a public act every disciple is called to take. After His resurrection, Jesus gave very specific instructions:

“All authority has been given to Me in heaven and on earth. Go therefore and make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things that I have commanded you; and lo, I am with you always, even to the end of the age.” (Matthew 28:18-20)

A command, coming from Jesus, is never an arbitrary chore. “If you love Me, keep My commandments,” He says (John 14:15): Christian obedience is a response of love, not a bureaucratic requirement. And notice the context of the command to baptize: it comes from the mouth of the Risen One, framed by two immense statements — “All authority has been given to Me” before, “I am with you always” after. The One who commands baptism is the One who conquered death and promises His presence: you can trust Him with a little water.

Look also at the example of Jesus Himself. At the Jordan, He is the one who comes to John the Baptist to be baptized — and John pulls back: “I need to be baptized by You!” Jesus insists: “Permit it to be so now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matthew 3:15). He, the sinless One, had no repentance to express; yet He stepped into the water to identify with us and open the way. If the Master saw fit to go through it, can the disciple consider it unnecessary?

When someone hesitates for a long time about baptism even though they've believed for years, the real question isn't “Is it mandatory?” but “What is keeping me from responding to the One who gave His life for me?” Often, the honest answer is fear of what others will think — precisely what baptism teaches us to move beyond. In Acts, notice the eagerness: the Ethiopian eunuch spots some water along the road and exclaims, “See, here is water. What hinders me from being baptized?” (Acts 8:36); the Philippian jailer is baptized “that same hour,” in the middle of the night (Acts 16:33). When the heart has understood, it doesn't negotiate deadlines.

sections.t: Examples of Baptism in the Bible
sections.p:
1. Jesus is baptized: (Matthew 3:13-17)

2. Jesus baptizes: (John 3:22-23)

3. Jesus teaches His disciples to baptize: (John 4:1-2)

4. Jesus commands baptism: (Mark 16:15-16; Matthew 28:19-20)

5. The Day of Pentecost: (Acts 2:37-41)

6. Philip in Samaria: (Acts 8:12-17)

7. The Ethiopian eunuch: (Acts 8:35-38)

8. Saul (Paul): (Acts 9:1-9)

9. Cornelius and his friends: (Acts 10:44-48)

10. The jailer and his family: (Acts 16:33)

11. The disciples in Ephesus: (Acts 19:1-7)

No. We are saved by God's grace, through faith in Jesus Christ, and not by an outward act. Repentance and faith in Christ are the keys to salvation: “For by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God.” (Ephesians 2:8)

Baptism is not a condition of salvation. Indeed, the Bible gives us the example of the criminal on the cross (Luke 23:32-43), who was not baptized but was saved nonetheless.

Here's an image to make it clear: baptism is to salvation what the wedding ring is to marriage. If a husband loses his ring at sea, he's still married; and wearing a ring bought at the market doesn't marry anyone. In the same way, the thief crucified next to Jesus entered paradise without baptism — he didn't have time — and on the other hand, going through the water without faith doesn't save: you go into the water dry and a sinner, and come out wet and a sinner. It is grace that saves, through faith.

Pause for a moment on that thief (Luke 23:39-43), because he is living proof of the Gospel. This man was not baptized, didn't take Communion, did no good works — his hands weren't free to do any; they were nailed down. All he had was faith: “Jesus, remember me when You come into Your kingdom.” And the answer comes, immediate and unconditional: “Today you will be with Me in Paradise.” Every theology of salvation must be able to pass the thief test: if your system requires something this man couldn't do, your system says more than the Gospel.

But be careful not to twist this grace the other way. The thief COULD NOT be baptized; someone who CAN be and keeps refusing is in a different situation: can you say “I do” in your heart and refuse to say it before witnesses? Obedience adds nothing to salvation — it is its signature. As James writes about works: faith that produces nothing should question its own vitality. Baptism doesn't save you; but if you are saved, why wait?

The essential conditions for baptism are faith and repentance:

— The one who has believed: (Mark 16:15-16)

— The one who has repented: (Acts 2:37-41)

— The one who has become a disciple: (Matthew 28:19-20)

Baptism is therefore reserved for people capable of making a conscious decision. There is no biblical example of infant baptism.

This question touches many people who were baptized as babies, often by sincere parents. Let's say it with respect: what their parents did carried the weight of a prayer and an intention — but biblical baptism calls for a personal response that no one can give in our place. Believe, repent, become a disciple: these are verbs you can only conjugate in the first person.

Look at the consistent pattern of the New Testament: in every baptism account in Acts, the order is the same — the Word is preached, the person believes, THEN they are baptized. “Those who gladly received his word were baptized” (Acts 2:41). Never the reverse, never by proxy. Even the faith of the most godly parents cannot believe on the child's behalf — it can bless them, guide them, pray for them (and that is precious: Timothy received the faith “which dwelt first” in his grandmother and his mother, 2 Timothy 1:5), but the day comes when each person answers for themselves.

So being baptized as an adult after being baptized as a child is not rejecting your family or “redoing” something: it is answering Jesus' call yourself, for the very first time. Many parents, far from being hurt, see it as the answer to the prayer they once spoke over their baby. If this is your situation, simply talk it over with a pastor — and if family tensions worry you, take time to explain your decision gently: you're not erasing your story, you're bringing it to its goal.

The word “baptize” comes from the Greek “baptizo,” which means to immerse, plunge, or submerge. To remain faithful to the biblical example, baptism should therefore be done by immersion.

The word baptizo belonged to the vocabulary of dyers: a cloth was “baptized” by plunging it completely into the dye vat. A beautiful detail: the cloth came out of the vat with a new color, permanently. That is the image God chose — not a minimal symbolic gesture, but a complete immersion from which you come out transformed, identified with Christ in His death and resurrection.

The biblical accounts confirm this meaning: John was baptizing at Aenon “because there was much water there” (John 3:23) — pointless if a few drops were enough; Jesus, after His baptism, “came up from the water” (Mark 1:10); Philip and the eunuch “both went down into the water” and then “came up out of” it (Acts 8:38-39). And only immersion tells the story baptism is meant to tell: you don't bury someone by sprinkling a handful of dirt on their forehead. Going all the way down speaks of the complete death of the old self; coming up speaks of resurrection.

Be reassured on one practical point: there's nothing to “get right.” All you have to do is let yourself be lowered and lifted up — and maybe that is the most beautiful lesson of the act: at the heart of the most important act of obedience in your life, you are passive in someone else's hands. Just like salvation itself.

Mark 16:15-16 shows the importance of publicly proclaiming your faith. This proclamation is evidence of sincerity and commitment to God. Jesus warned that the fear of people must never outweigh our desire to please God (John 12:42-43).

Being baptized doesn't require exhaustive knowledge of the Bible, but it does require a commitment to follow Jesus as Lord. Baptism is for those who have decided to become part of God's Kingdom.

“Not everyone who says to Me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ shall enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of My Father in heaven.” (Matthew 7:21)

Look at our day and age: nobody is ashamed to display their football team, their favorite artist, or their company on their clothes and social media. We publicly proclaim a thousand allegiances. Baptism asks the question: and what about Jesus? Paul wrote: “I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God to salvation for everyone who believes” (Romans 1:16).

Jesus spoke a solemn word about this: “Whoever confesses Me before men, him I will also confess before My Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 10:32). Consider the exchange: you acknowledge Him before people — coworkers, cousins, neighbors — and He acknowledges you before the Father and His angels. There's no better deal in the universe. Baptism is the first great opportunity for this public confession.

A very practical tip: make your baptism a celebration and your first act of evangelism. Invite your family, your friends, your coworkers — including, and especially, those who don't believe. Many people heard the Gospel for the first time at a loved one's baptism, listening to their testimony: a baptism intrigues, moves, disarms — you can't argue with a changed life. Prepare a few simple sentences: who I was, how I met Jesus, what He has changed. Two minutes is enough. That day, your life preaches better than a sermon — and the meal afterward is worth many meetings.

A disciple, though aware of their weaknesses, relies on God's grace to grow in sanctification and conform to God's will. Baptism marks a turning point where the disciple chooses to leave the old life behind and walk with Christ.

“And they continued steadfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and in prayers.” (Acts 2:42)

Baptism is therefore an act of obedience, love, and faith toward God. It testifies to our desire to walk in newness of life, to belong to the Church, and to live as true disciples of Jesus Christ.

Let's be clear to avoid a trap: baptism commits you to a direction, not to perfection. A baptized person isn't someone who never falls anymore; it's someone who, when they fall, now falls forward — toward Christ — and gets back up by His grace.

Peter is the comforting proof. After years of walking with Jesus, even after Pentecost, Paul still has to rebuke him publicly in Antioch for hypocrisy (Galatians 2:11-14) — and Peter accepts the correction, and grows. The same man would later write: “Grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord” (2 Peter 3:18). Grow: a gardener's word, not a judge's. God isn't looking for flawless trophies; He is cultivating living trees.

What matters is the deep orientation of the heart. A boat can be tossed by the waves and pushed off course by currents: as long as its heading stays fixed on the harbor, it moves forward. Baptism has set your course. So when you fall — and you will — don't stay on the ground accusing yourself: “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9). Confess quickly, get up quickly, move on quickly. Biblical holiness isn't the absence of falls; it's refusing to camp there.

Baptism is much more than a simple religious rite or a Christian tradition. It is a fundamental act of obedience, a public testimony of faith, and a response to Jesus' direct command.

By following His example and His teachings, we understand that baptism symbolizes a profound transformation: the passage from spiritual death to new life in Christ. It is a visible commitment to God, a proclamation of our faith, and a declaration that we belong to the Body of Christ, the Church.

Though baptism is not a means of salvation, it is a sign of genuine faith and sincere repentance. It expresses the will to live by God's grace and to walk in newness of life.

So through baptism, the disciple affirms their decision to leave the old life behind to follow Jesus, to be united with Him in His death and resurrection, and to live fully under the Lordship of Christ. May this act of love and faith remain a source of blessing and encouragement for all who choose to answer Jesus' call.

lecons.engagement:
I commit to obey the call of Jesus Christ by being baptized, recognizing this act as a public proclamation of my faith and a symbol of my new life in Him.

I commit to live in newness of life, renouncing my old nature to walk according to God's will.

I also commit to follow the teachings of Jesus, to acknowledge Him as my Lord and Savior, and to live a life that reflects His love, His grace, and His truth. Through my baptism, I testify that I belong to the kingdom of God and that I desire to grow as a disciple.

Finally, I commit to persevere in the faith, to walk in fellowship with the Church, and to proclaim the Gospel through my life and my actions, so that God may be glorified in all things.
application: Prepare for baptism: study the Bible passages on baptism and talk with a pastor to fully understand its meaning
Plan your baptism: choose a date, involve your local church, and invite your loved ones to witness your commitment
Live in newness of life: maintain a deep relationship with God through prayer, Bible reading, and a life led by the Holy Spirit
Get involved in the Church: join a ministry or a group to serve and grow alongside other believers
Be a living testimony: live by Jesus' teachings and share your faith with those around you
Persevere in your commitment: pray for strength to stay faithful and surround yourself with Christians who will support you in your walk
Through these actions, you will reflect your commitment to God and the meaning of your baptism as a new life in Christ — “Walk in newness of life” (Romans 6:4)

quiz.q: What does immersion in water symbolize?
choix: The death of the old life and resurrection with Christ
quiz.explication: “We were buried with Him through baptism into death… that we also should walk in newness of life” (Romans 6:4).

quiz.q: Does baptism save?
choix: Yes, it is the condition for salvation
Yes, if it's done by immersion
No: we are saved by grace, through faith
quiz.explication: The criminal on the cross was saved without baptism (Luke 23:43). Baptism testifies to salvation received; it doesn't produce it (Ephesians 2:8).

quiz.q: Who can be baptized?
choix: The one who has believed and repented
quiz.explication: The biblical conditions: believe (Mark 16:16), repent (Acts 2:38), become a disciple (Matthew 28:19) — a conscious decision.

quiz.q: What does the Greek word “baptizo” mean?
quiz.explication: Hence the biblical practice of baptism by full immersion.

quiz.q: Why is baptism a PUBLIC act?
choix: Because it openly proclaims one's faith and commitment
quiz.explication: It is a public testimony of sincerity (Mark 16:15-16) — the fear of people must not outweigh the desire to please God (John 12:42-43).

quiz.q: What is baptism compared to in this lesson?
choix: A wedding ring: it doesn't create love, it proclaims it publicly
A purification rite inherited from the Law
quiz.explication: Like a ring placed on the finger before witnesses, baptism doesn't produce salvation: it publicly proclaims a heart that already belongs to Christ — and it is a commitment.

quiz.q: Which biblical example shows that a person can be saved without being baptized?
choix: The criminal crucified next to Jesus (Luke 23)
quiz.explication: The thief on the cross had no time to be baptized, yet Jesus promised him paradise: it is grace that saves, through faith.

quiz.q: In Matthew 28:18-20, what does Jesus command His disciples?
choix: To build temples in every city
To make disciples of all nations and baptize them in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit
To wait for His return in Jerusalem
To baptize only the people of Israel
quiz.explication: This is the risen Lord's missionary command: make disciples, baptize them, and teach them to observe everything He commanded.

quiz.q: Why is infant baptism not the biblical example followed here?
choix: Because the water would be dangerous for a baby
Because the Bible explicitly forbids it
Because baptism requires a conscious decision: to believe and repent for oneself
Because it's a matter of legal age
quiz.explication: Believe, repent, become a disciple: verbs you can only conjugate in the first person. There is no biblical example of infant baptism.

quiz.q: Among Greek dyers, what happened to the cloth “baptized” (baptizo) in the vat?
choix: It came out with a new color, permanently
It was hung out to dry
quiz.explication: The immersed cloth came out transformed for good — the very picture of identification with Christ: you go down, you are buried, you rise to a new life.

lecons.resume: The bread and the cup: remembering the sacrifice, proclaiming His death, living in communion.

sections.t: The Origin of the Lord's Supper
sections.p:
Originally, the first Lord's Supper took place during an actual meal that Jesus shared with His disciples on the day the Jewish Passover was celebrated. This meal preceded the arrest of Jesus Christ in the Garden of Gethsemane, which in turn preceded the crucifixion of Jesus.

God had commanded that this feast commemorate the deliverance He had accomplished for His people when they were slaves in Egypt; at that time, the blood of a lamb applied to the doorway of each Israelite home had saved them from God's judgment (Exodus 12). From then on, every year in Israel, people ate unleavened bread for seven days and sacrificed a lamb to commemorate this event, which in a way sealed God's covenant with His people. So it is no accident that Jesus chose this highly symbolic moment to announce the new covenant God had promised, and to die.

“And as they were eating, Jesus took bread, blessed and broke it, and gave it to the disciples and said, ‘Take, eat; this is My body.’ Then He took the cup, and gave thanks, and gave it to them, saying, ‘Drink from it, all of you. For this is My blood of the covenant, which is shed for many for the remission of sins. I tell you, I will not drink of this fruit of the vine from now on until that day when I drink it new with you in My Father's kingdom.’ And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.” (Matthew 26:26-30)

To grasp the significance of this scene, we need to picture the Passover meal as Jesus had experienced it since childhood. Every year, the family gathered around the roasted lamb, the unleavened bread, and the bitter herbs, and the youngest asked the ritual question: “Why is this night different from all other nights?” Then the father would tell the story: the slavery in Egypt, the lamb's blood on the doors, the angel of judgment who “passes over” the marked houses, freedom in the morning. Every element of the meal spoke: the bitter herbs recalled the bitterness of slavery, the unleavened bread the haste of departure, the lamb the price of deliverance.

And that evening, in the middle of this age-old meal, Jesus takes the bread and dares to say, “This is My body.” Consider the boldness: He places Himself at the center of Israel's founding story. He identifies Himself as the true Lamb, of whom all the Passover lambs were only a foreshadowing—exactly what John the Baptist had proclaimed when he saw Him: “Behold! The Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29). Paul would put it in one sentence: “Christ, our Passover, was sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). The blood on the doors saved from a judgment; His blood saves from THE judgment.

One detail is overwhelming when you think about it: the people in the marked houses were not spared because they were better than others—but solely because of the blood on the door. The question that night was not “Are you a good person?” but “Are you under the blood?” It is still the only question that matters.

“Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah—not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day that I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt, My covenant which they broke, though I was a husband to them, says the Lord. But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord: I will put My law in their minds, and write it on their hearts; and I will be their God, and they shall be My people. No more shall every man teach his neighbor, and every man his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord,’ for they all shall know Me, from the least of them to the greatest of them, says the Lord. For I will forgive their iniquity, and their sin I will remember no more.” (Jeremiah 31:31-34)

By asking His disciples to share this meal in remembrance of Him, Jesus wants them, too, to remember the deliverance He came to bring them at the cost of His own life—He, the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29; 1 Peter 1:18-19). His disciples would need to remember this regularly throughout their lives.

Let's pause on this word “covenant,” because our age misunderstands it. A contract protects interests: each party commits to certain obligations, and if one fails, the other is released. A covenant binds persons: “I am yours, you are mine,” for better or for worse. Marriage is a covenant; a phone plan is a contract.

The whole Bible is the story of God's covenants—with Noah, Abraham, Moses, David—and of a recurring problem: God remains faithful, but man doesn't keep his part. The covenant of Sinai, engraved in stone, was holy and good; but it remained outside of man, like a road sign that shows the way without supplying the fuel. Israel broke it even before Moses came down from the mountain. Something else was needed—not a better law, but a better heart.

That is exactly what Jeremiah foretells: a new covenant, written no longer on tablets of stone but “on their hearts.” The difference is immense: God no longer merely tells us what to do—He places within us, by His Spirit, the desire and the strength to do it (this is what Ezekiel 36:26-27 promises in parallel: a new heart AND His Spirit within us). And forgiveness no longer has to be renewed endlessly through sacrifices: “Their sin I will remember no more.”

At every Communion, that is the cup you lift. Not “I'll try to earn Your love better this week,” but “Your love has purchased me, Your Spirit dwells in me, Your forgiveness is final.” The Lord's Supper is the memorial of a covenant in which God Himself guarantees both sides—that is why it is a celebration and not a source of anxiety.

sections.t: The Institution of the Lord's Supper
sections.p:
In this passage, Paul establishes the celebration of the Lord's Supper in the church at Corinth, and consequently in all churches:

“For I received from the Lord that which I also delivered to you: that the Lord Jesus on the same night in which He was betrayed took bread; and when He had given thanks, He broke it and said, ‘Take, eat; this is My body which is broken for you; do this in remembrance of Me.’ In the same manner He also took the cup after supper, saying, ‘This cup is the new covenant in My blood. This do, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of Me.’ For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord's death till He comes. Therefore whoever eats this bread or drinks this cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of the bread and drink of the cup. For he who eats and drinks in an unworthy manner eats and drinks judgment to himself, not discerning the Lord's body. For this reason many are weak and sick among you, and many sleep.” (1 Corinthians 11:23-30)

Along with baptism, the Lord's Supper is one of the two “sacraments” instituted by the Lord for His disciples. There are no others in the New Testament.

The “breaking of bread” was to take place during the worship service. So for them, continuing steadfastly in the breaking of bread meant their commitment to this great gathering of the whole church assembled to praise God and to remember the death of Jesus Christ.

Several words and expressions have been used to refer to the commemoration of Jesus' last meal with His disciples: terms such as “communion” or “Eucharist,” which means thanksgiving. The Bible simply speaks of the Lord's table and the breaking of bread: “And they continued steadfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and in prayers.” (Acts 2:42; see also Acts 20:7). The French word “Cène,” for its part, simply means meal or supper.

The main reference texts for the Lord's Supper are: Matthew 26:26-30, Mark 14:22-25, Luke 22:14-20, and 1 Corinthians 11:23-26.

“Do this in remembrance of Me.” In the Bible, remembrance is much more than nostalgic recollection. When Israel remembered the Passover, each generation said, “It is I whom God brought out of Egypt”—the past event became present and active. In the same way, the Lord's Supper is not a moment of silence before an old photograph: it is a meal where the crucified and risen One is alive among His own, and where His work is applied to us today.

A couple celebrating their wedding anniversary doesn't just reminisce: by repeating the gestures of love—the meal, the words, sometimes the place—they renew their present commitment. That is what the Church does at the Lord's table: it renews the covenant, “till He comes.”

Notice also to whom Paul writes these lines: to the church at Corinth, a community full of divisions, disorder, and scandals—not an assembly of perfect people. And he doesn't tell them, “Stop taking Communion until further notice,” but “Take it in a worthy manner.” The Lord's table has always been set in the midst of imperfect churches: it is not the reward of the blameless; it is the meeting place of the redeemed.

One last detail that gives you chills: “the Lord Jesus, ON THE SAME NIGHT IN WHICH HE WAS BETRAYED, took bread… and gave thanks.” He knew—Judas had already gone out into the night—and He gave thanks. Facing the worst night in history, Jesus opened His hands and gave thanks. Every Communion teaches us this way of walking through our own nights.

sections.t: The Meaning of the Lord's Supper
sections.p:
Like baptism, the Lord's Supper invites us to look to the cross where Jesus gave His life: the bread represents His crucified body, and the wine recalls His shed blood. By partaking of them, Christians remember the price Jesus paid for their redemption: His death. They also proclaim His resurrection, for they partake while awaiting His return and the feast of the Lamb.

“For I say to you, I will not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes… that you may eat and drink at My table in My kingdom, and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” (Luke 22:18, 30; see also Revelation 19:9)

The Lord's Supper is not merely a symbol. It calls upon our faith. It is by faith that we know Jesus is present among us and that we experience real fellowship with our brothers and sisters in Jesus. It is also through our faith that the Holy Spirit enables us to take full possession of everything the Lord obtained for us by dying on the cross for us: our forgiveness, our healing, our deliverance.

“But He was wounded for our transgressions, He was bruised for our iniquities; the chastisement for our peace was upon Him, and by His stripes we are healed.” (Isaiah 53:5)

The Bible never speaks of a miracle in which the substance of the elements changes at the moment of the celebration. The bread and the wine remain what they are, but at the same time they bear witness to a living reality that goes beyond them: Jesus, who died and rose again, truly present and alive in us and among us.

The Bible gives no further details about celebrating the Lord's Supper, such as its frequency, its manner, or its date. Each church is therefore called to adapt its practice to its context, according to the deep meaning of the Lord's Supper that it perceives and that governs the practical aspects. It would therefore be a mistake to judge Christians who practice it somewhat differently from us, for life with God is above all a matter of love, obedience, and faith. The Lord's Supper is a means to help us in that. It is not an end in itself.

Notice God's way of teaching: He could have simply asked us to think about the cross. Instead, He chose a meal, which engages all the senses—the bread you hold, break, and taste; the cup you bring to your lips. God knows our nature: we are not pure spirits, and truths that pass through the body are imprinted more deeply than those that remain ideas. That is why the Lord's Supper also reaches those going through seasons when they don't “feel” anything: even when emotion is absent, the act proclaims, and faith leans on the act.

Note the biblical balance between two extremes. On one hand, the Lord's Supper is not a magical act in which the bread changes substance—the Bible never speaks of such a miracle. On the other, it is not merely an empty memory, a ceremony of the past: Paul speaks of “the communion of the blood of Christ… the communion of the body of Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:16)—the Greek word is koinōnia, a real participation. By faith, the Risen One is present and active at His table: forgiveness sealed, hearts healed, relationships restored.

And don't forget which way to look: the Lord's Supper looks back (to the cross), around (to the brothers and sisters with whom we share the same bread—“we, though many, are one body; for we all partake of that one bread,” 1 Corinthians 10:17), and FORWARD: “till He comes.” Every Communion is a dress rehearsal for the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9). Around the table, the Church has its back turned to Egypt and its face turned toward the Kingdom.

The biblical term “communion” also shows that the Lord's Supper cannot be taken lightly: it bears witness to our communion with God and with our brothers and sisters. The apostle Paul speaks of the possibility of taking the Lord's Supper “in an unworthy manner.” What do you think that means?

It would be wrong to take part in this meal if we are not in genuine communion with God and with one another. That is what was happening in Corinth: “For in eating, each one takes his own supper ahead of others; and one is hungry and another is drunk.” (1 Corinthians 11:21)

“Therefore whoever eats this bread or drinks this cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of the bread and drink of the cup. For he who eats and drinks without discerning the Lord's body eats and drinks judgment to himself. For this reason many are weak and sick among you, and many sleep.” (1 Corinthians 11:27-30)

“Therefore if you bring your gift to the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.” (Matthew 5:23-24)

Yet it would be a serious mistake to keep depriving yourself of Holy Communion without seeking to make things right with God and with your brothers and sisters. God wants us to remember the price of our salvation: His love revealed through Jesus' sacrifice on the cross.

What attitudes should fill a Christian's heart when taking part in Holy Communion? “Love does not behave rudely, does not seek its own, is not provoked, thinks no evil.” (1 Corinthians 13:5)

One word here sets many anxious Christians free: Paul speaks of taking the Lord's Supper “unworthily”—in an unworthy manner. It's an adverb, describing a way of doing something, not an adjective describing unworthy people. After all, who could ever be “worthy” of Christ's sacrifice? No one. The Lord's table isn't set for the perfect, but for forgiven sinners. If you wait until you're worthy to come, you'll never come; if you understand that it's for those hungry for grace, you'll run to it.

In Corinth, the problem wasn't that imperfect people were taking part: it was that people were taking part without love. Picture the scene: the Lord's Supper was shared during a real community meal. The wealthy, arriving early, ate and drank among themselves to the point of drunkenness, while the slaves and laborers, arriving late, found the dishes empty and went hungry—and then everyone “celebrated” the memorial of the One who gave His body for all. That is the unworthiness Paul condemns: approaching the sacrifice of love while trampling on your brothers and sisters.

Self-examination, then, is a mirror, not a barrier. Before Communion, ask yourself two simple questions: Am I at peace with God? Am I at peace with my brothers and sisters? If there's a grudge, a conflict, a word that needs to be made right—first go and be reconciled, Jesus says, then come. Many churches have seen real reconciliations happen precisely because Communion was coming up: brothers estranged for months finally talking on Sunday morning. It's one of its most precious fruits—the Lord's table cleans house in our relationships like nothing else.

And if, on the other hand, you find yourself avoiding Communion month after month out of a sense of unworthiness: now is the time to talk with a leader. Staying away from the remedy because you know you're sick is the exact opposite of the Gospel.

Holy Communion is far more than a mere rite or Christian tradition: it is an invitation to remember, to proclaim, and to live in communion with Jesus Christ and with our brothers and sisters. As we share the bread and the wine, we recall Jesus' ultimate sacrifice on the cross, His body given and His blood shed for the forgiveness of our sins. This act, filled with faith and love, brings us back to what matters most: the grace of God, the power of the cross, and the hope of His return.

It is also a call to self-examination and reconciliation. The Lord's Supper reminds us that our communion with God cannot be separated from our communion with others. Taking part in this meal in a spirit of faith, gratitude, and reconciliation allows us to fully experience the power of Christ's work in our lives.

So Holy Communion is not simply a moment of quiet reflection, but a living experience of Christ's presence among us. By obeying this command of the Lord, we affirm our devotion to Him, our gratitude for His sacrifice, and our desire to walk in His light until His glorious return.

lecons.engagement:
I commit to taking part in Holy Communion with faith, reverence, and gratitude, remembering Jesus Christ's sacrifice for the forgiveness of my sins.

I commit to examining my heart, to reconciling with my brothers and sisters when needed, and to sharing this meal in communion with God and the Church. Through this act, I proclaim my faith in Christ, my gratitude for His love, and my determination to walk in obedience to His Word as I await His glorious return.
application: Take part with faith and gratitude: approach Holy Communion acknowledging the sacrifice of Jesus Christ and expressing your gratitude
Examine your heart: take time to confess your sins and repent before taking part
Live in reconciliation: seek to resolve any conflict or disagreement with your brothers and sisters before taking part
Understand its deeper meaning: meditate on the biblical texts to grasp the significance of the bread and the wine as symbols of Christ's body and blood
Take part regularly: commit to not neglecting this important moment of communion with God and the Church
Live in hope: take Communion with a heart full of gratitude and expectation for Christ's return

Embrace a transformed way of life: make this commitment a daily reality by walking in love, forgiveness, and holiness. These steps will help you experience Holy Communion fully and in line with God's will

quiz.q: During which feast did Jesus institute the Lord's Supper?
quiz.explication: The Passover meal commemorated the deliverance from Egypt through the blood of the lamb (Exodus 12)—Jesus, the Lamb of God, inaugurates the new covenant there.

quiz.q: What do the bread and the cup represent?
choix: Food shared among brothers and sisters
Jesus' crucified body and shed blood
quiz.explication: “This is My body… this is My blood of the new covenant, which is shed for many for the remission of sins” (Matthew 26:26-28).

quiz.q: What do we proclaim when we take the Lord's Supper?
choix: The Lord's death, until He comes
quiz.explication: 1 Corinthians 11:26: “you proclaim the Lord's death till He comes”—remembrance AND hope.

quiz.q: What should you do before taking part in the Lord's Supper?
choix: Examine yourself and be reconciled if needed
quiz.explication: “Let a man examine himself” (1 Corinthians 11:28)—and be reconciled first (Matthew 5:23-24).

quiz.q: How many “sacraments” did the Lord institute in the New Testament?
choix: Two: baptism and the Lord's Supper
quiz.explication: Along with baptism, Holy Communion is one of only two sacraments Jesus instituted for His disciples.

quiz.q: What event did the Jewish Passover commemorate?
choix: The deliverance from Egypt, when the blood of the lamb protected the houses (Exodus 12)
The entry into the Promised Land
quiz.explication: Every year, Israel remembered the night when the lamb's blood on the doorposts saved them. Jesus is “our Passover” (1 Corinthians 5:7): the true Lamb.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a contract and a covenant?
choix: A contract protects interests; a covenant binds persons
A covenant is written, a contract is oral
A contract is religious, a covenant is civil
quiz.explication: A subscription is a contract; marriage is a covenant: “I am yours, you are mine.” At the Lord's Supper, we raise the cup of the new covenant, written on the heart.

quiz.q: What does it mean to take the Lord's Supper “unworthily”?
choix: To take it when you are an unworthy person
To take it in an unworthy manner—without love, without self-examination, without reconciliation
To take it without being a church member
quiz.explication: “Unworthily” is an adverb: it describes a way of doing something, not people. The Lord's table is for forgiven sinners—self-examination is a mirror, not a barrier.

quiz.q: What does the Bible say about the exact frequency and manner of celebrating the Lord's Supper?
choix: It requires a celebration every week
It restricts it to Passover evening
It doesn't set these details: each church adapts according to the deeper meaning of the Lord's Supper
It calls for celebrating it once a year
quiz.explication: The Bible specifies no frequency, date, or method: it would be wrong to judge Christians who practice it differently—the Lord's Supper is a means, not an end in itself.

quiz.q: Based on Jeremiah 31:31-34, where is the new covenant written?
choix: On a scroll kept in Jerusalem
quiz.explication: “I will put My law in their minds, and write it on their hearts”: God doesn't just tell us what to do—by His Spirit, He puts within us the desire and the strength to do it.

lecons.resume: Giving with joy: an act of worship, faith, and gratitude toward God.

sections.t: Definition and Origin of the Tithe
sections.p:
The word tithe literally means “tenth part.” The first mention of the tithe in the Bible appears when Abraham chooses to offer it to God in gratitude for the victory He gave him over his enemies:

“And blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand! And Abraham gave him a tithe of all.” (Genesis 14:20)

Later, after the dream of the ladder, Jacob vows to give God a tenth of everything he will receive from Him:

“Then Jacob made a vow, saying, If God will be with me, and keep me in this way that I am going, and give me bread to eat and clothing to put on, so that I come back to my father's house in peace, then the Lord shall be my God. And this stone which I have set as a pillar shall be God's house, and of all that You give me I will surely give a tenth to You.” (Genesis 28:20-22)

Later still, in the Law given to Israel, the tithe was established as a divine command:

“You shall truly tithe all the increase of your grain that the field produces year by year. And you shall eat before the Lord your God, in the place where He chooses to make His name abide, the tithe of your grain and your new wine and your oil, of the firstborn of your herds and your flocks, that you may learn to fear the Lord your God always.” (Deuteronomy 14:22-23)

Let's make it very concrete: the tithe is one tenth. On an income of $1,500, that's $150; on $800, it's $80. The principle has a particular beauty: it's proportional, so the same step of trust is asked of everyone, whatever their standard of living.

But pause on one decisive detail: the first two tithes in the Bible—Abraham's and Jacob's—were given BEFORE the Law, centuries before Moses. No one required it of them; no command existed yet. Abraham gives a tithe to Melchizedek in response to a victory God had just given him; Jacob promises it in response to a promise God had just made him. So the tithe is born as a reflex of gratitude, not as a tax—and that's why it spans the ages: it doesn't belong to the system of the Law, it belongs to the grammar of a grateful heart.

The second detail is the word “firstfruits”: the first fruits, not the leftovers. Israel brought the first sheaf of the harvest—before knowing what the rest of the field would yield. Giving first or giving what's left: those are two opposing theologies. The first says, “God is my priority and my security”; the second, “God will get whatever my expenses happen to leave Him.” Here's a test that doesn't lie: look at a bank statement and a calendar—better than any speech, they reveal what holds first place in a life. Jesus put it in one sentence: “For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:21). Notice the order: He doesn't say your money will follow your heart, but that your heart will follow your money. Put your treasure in the Kingdom, and your heart will hold fast to it.

sections.t: The Reasons for the Tithe in the Old Testament
sections.p:
1. Acknowledging God’s sovereignty. By giving the tithe, believers acknowledge that everything comes from God: health, work, family, prosperity.

2. Trusting God. Giving a portion of one’s resources, even in difficult circumstances, shows complete dependence on God.

“Bring all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be food in My house, and try Me now in this, says the Lord of hosts, if I will not open for you the windows of heaven and pour out for you such blessing that there will not be room enough to receive it.” (Malachi 3:10-12)

3. Supporting the service of God. The tithe was used to sustain the Levites, the men consecrated to God’s service, and to support worship. When there was slackness, God’s servants abandoned their ministry, and idolatry took hold (2 Chronicles 29:9).

In addition to the tithe, God encouraged His people to give freely as their hearts moved them. These offerings were used for specific projects, such as building the tabernacle or the temple (Exodus 35:21-29). These seasons of generosity often coincided with spiritual revivals, when the people rediscovered the joy of worshiping and serving God.

Generosity toward the poor: the Mosaic Law included specific instructions for helping those most in need, encouraging generosity and preventing poverty from taking root among the people.

“Six years you shall sow your land and gather in its produce, but the seventh year you shall let it rest and lie fallow, that the poor of your people may eat; and what they leave, the beasts of the field may eat.” (Exodus 23:10-11)

Jesus did not abolish the tithe, but He invited His disciples to go beyond it, teaching them to give with a sincere heart.

“Jesus sat opposite the treasury and saw how the people put money into the treasury. And many who were rich put in much. Then one poor widow came and threw in two mites… Jesus said: This poor widow has put in more than all, for she put in all that she had, her whole livelihood.” (Mark 12:41-44)

The scene of the widow overturns our calculations. Picture yourself in the temple: the offering boxes were large, trumpet-shaped metal receptacles, and the coins rang out inside them — the bigger the gift, the louder it sounded. The rich made their offerings ring; a widow slips in two lepta, the smallest coins in existence, barely a clink. And Jesus, sitting across from it, calls His disciples over: she has given “more than all.” Why? Because God doesn’t count what we give, but what we keep: the rich gave out of their surplus; she gave “her whole livelihood.” God looks at what’s left, not at the amount.

Notice too what this scene reveals: Jesus watches what people give — and He isn’t embarrassed by it. Our culture considers money the most private subject there is; Jesus talks about it more often than about prayer, precisely because nothing reveals the heart better.

Let’s correct a widespread distortion here: giving is not a business transaction with God. We don’t “pay” God to get blessings, like putting a coin in a vending machine — those who preach this turn grace into commerce. The promises of Malachi 3 are real: God honors faithfulness, and generations of Christians testify to it. But the meaning of Christian giving is gratitude, not calculation: we give because we have already received everything in Christ — “He who did not spare His own Son… how shall He not with Him also freely give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). You don’t bribe a Father who has already given everything.

The offering is an integral part of Christian worship. It would be inconsistent for a believer under grace to give less than under the Law. God was infinitely generous in giving His Son for us:

“For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, that you through His poverty might become rich.” (2 Corinthians 8:9)

The giver’s attitude: the Christian should give joyfully and without compulsion.

“So let each one give as he purposes in his heart, not grudgingly or of necessity; for God loves a cheerful giver.” (2 Corinthians 9:7)

“But when you do a charitable deed, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing.” (Matthew 6:3-4)

A piece of advice proven by many Christians: decide in advance, then automate. Paul already gave the Corinthians this plan: “On the first day of the week let each one of you lay something aside, storing up as he may prosper” (1 Corinthians 16:2) — a regular rhythm, a set portion, right from the start. In practical terms today: set up an automatic transfer on the day your income arrives, before your account melts away over the month. This doesn’t take the heart out of the gesture; it protects it: the decision was made in prayer, once, calmly; carrying it out no longer depends on moods or surprises.

And what about difficult financial seasons? Look at the Macedonians, whom Paul praises: “In a great trial of affliction the abundance of their joy and their deep poverty abounded in the riches of their liberality. For I bear witness that according to their ability, yes, and beyond their ability, they were freely willing” (2 Corinthians 8:2-3). Poor people joyful to give — that shatters the idea that generosity is reserved for the rich. The Bible asks no one to go into debt in order to give; but it shows that the joy of giving doesn’t depend on your balance. Even a small gift, given faithfully in hard times, is an act of faith that says: “My security isn’t my account, it’s my Father.”

Finally, keep the compass of 2 Corinthians 9:7: “not grudgingly or of necessity; for God loves a cheerful giver.” If your gift is being wrung out of you by guilt or pressure, stop, and bring the question back before God until the joy returns: He prefers a smaller gift given joyfully to a large one given reluctantly.

sections.t: The Tithe: An Act of Worship
sections.p:
Giving the tithe is an act of gratitude and faith:

— An act of faith: the one who gives acknowledges that God will provide for all their needs.

— Support for the work of the Church: tithes and offerings enable the Church to function and to support missionary work around the world.

— A source of joy and praise: “They glorify God for the obedience of your confession to the gospel of Christ, and for your liberal sharing with them.” (2 Corinthians 9:13)

A key to understanding why money is such a spiritual subject: your money is your life’s time, crystallized. Those hours of work, that fatigue, those skills — all of it has been converted into numbers in an account. So giving money is literally giving part of your life. That’s why the offering given on Sunday isn’t just a line item in the service: it is an act of worship just as much as singing — perhaps even more demanding, because singing costs nothing.

David said something on this subject that should be engraved on our wallets. When he is offered Araunah’s threshing floor for free to build an altar, he refuses: “Nor will I offer burnt offerings to the Lord my God with that which costs me nothing” (2 Samuel 24:24). Worship that costs nothing says something about how much we value God. By contrast, Mary of Bethany breaks over Jesus a perfume worth a year’s wages — the disciples cry waste, and Jesus declares that her act will be told throughout the whole world (Mark 14:3-9). Worship gladly “wastes” itself on the one it loves: just ask anyone in love.

And remember who you got what you give from. David again, on the day of the offerings for the temple: “All things come from You, and of Your own we have given You” (1 Chronicles 29:14). Giving doesn’t impoverish the giver: it puts them back in the truth — a richly blessed steward of a generous God who owns it all.

sections.t: The Example of the Early Church
sections.p:
The Church of the first Christians was marked by great generosity and true fellowship:

“Now all who believed were together, and had all things in common, and sold their possessions and goods, and divided them among all, as anyone had need.” (Acts 2:44-47)

This generosity is no distant utopia: it is still lived out today. In our churches, it has a thousand concrete faces — meals brought to a mom who just gave birth, a quiet collection to cover the bill of an unemployed brother, a car lent, a home opened to a student. And the text of Acts notes the result: “the Lord added to the church daily those who were being saved.” The generosity of the first Christians was their best sermon: the world couldn’t explain these people.

History confirmed it spectacularly: in the fourth century, Emperor Julian — nicknamed the Apostate, who wanted to restore paganism — complained in a now-famous letter that the “impious Galileans” fed not only their own poor but the pagans’ poor as well, putting his religion to shame. The enemy of Christianity unwittingly testified to its greatest proof. No argument has ever converted as many people as the generosity of Christians.

Finally, notice the balance of the text: “they sold their possessions AS ANYONE HAD NEED” — it was neither mandatory communism (Peter would tell Ananias that his field remained his own, Acts 5:4) nor every man for himself: a joyful freedom guided by real needs. That’s the model: not a percentage that settles our duty, but eyes open to the needs around us, and hands that follow.

Tithes and offerings are much more than a mere religious practice: they are an act of worship, faith, and gratitude toward God. By giving, we affirm that everything we own comes from Him, and we express our trust in His ability to provide for all our needs.

These gifts support the work of the Church, foster unity and fellowship among believers, and make it possible to meet the needs of those most in need. As Jesus taught, true giving isn’t measured by quantity, but by the sincerity of the heart.

By embracing the spirit of generosity that characterized the early Church, we bear witness to God’s goodness and to the impact of His grace in our lives. Giving joyfully and in love is a concrete way to glorify God and to take part in the advancement of His Kingdom.

“Bring all the tithes into the storehouse… and I will pour out for you such blessing in abundance.” (Malachi 3:10-12)

lecons.engagement:
I commit to honoring God with my tithes and offerings, acknowledging that everything I own comes from Him.

I commit to giving faithfully and with a joyful heart, not out of obligation, but out of love and gratitude toward my Lord.

I also commit to supporting God’s work through the Church, taking part in the advancement of His Kingdom and contributing to the needs of those most in need. Through my giving, I proclaim my faith in God’s provision and my desire to see His Name glorified.

Finally, I commit to living in generosity and trust, knowing that God abundantly blesses those who give with sincerity and devotion, according to His promise in Malachi 3:10.
application: Recognize that everything comes from God: take time to meditate on the blessings God gives you — your life, your resources, your work, and even the small daily provisions. This will strengthen your motivation to give as an act of gratitude

Establish a regular discipline: set a time each month (or according to your income) to set aside your tithe, that is, one tenth of your income, and to decide the amount of your offerings. Make it a spiritual habit, following the example of Abraham’s or Jacob’s faithfulness
Give with a joyful heart: never give out of compulsion or guilt. Before giving, pray that God will align your heart with His will and fill you with joy at the thought of contributing to His work

Support the Church and others in practical ways: identify the specific needs of your local church — building upkeep, support for pastors or missionaries, charitable projects. You can also plan additional offerings to help those in need

Plan and organize your giving: set aside a portion of your budget for tithes and offerings. By being intentional, you’ll avoid giving sporadically or on impulse, and you’ll honor your commitment consistently

Rely on faith, not fear: when you give, trust God’s promise that He will provide for your needs (Malachi 3:10). Even in times of financial hardship, remember that giving is an act of faith, not a matter of surplus
Practice generosity in every area: beyond money, be generous with your time, your talents, and your love toward others. Adopt a giver’s mindset in your daily life, reflecting God’s generous character

Reevaluate and pray regularly: take time to reexamine your giving practice in light of Scripture and your blessings. Ask God to guide you in your giving so that it is always aligned with His will and done with a sincere heart. By applying these principles, your commitment to giving tithes and offerings will become a living testimony of your love for God and your faith in His faithfulness

quiz.q: What does the word “tithe” mean?
quiz.explication: Literally “tenth part” — practiced by Abraham (Genesis 14:20) long before the Law.

quiz.q: Who was the first to give a tithe in the Bible?
quiz.explication: Abraham gave a tithe of everything after his victory (Genesis 14:20); Jacob later made the same vow (Genesis 28:22).

quiz.q: In Malachi 3:10, what does God promise to those who bring the tithe?
choix: To open the windows of heaven and pour out blessing
quiz.explication: “Try Me now in this… and see if I will not open for you the windows of heaven.”

quiz.q: What did Jesus teach through the poor widow?
choix: That you must give away all your money
That the rich always give better
That the value of a gift is measured by the heart, not the amount
That the temple treasury was useless
quiz.explication: “She has put in more than all” (Mark 12:43-44): two small coins, but her whole heart.

quiz.q: How does God want us to give?
choix: Cheerfully, not grudgingly or under compulsion
By letting everyone know about it
Only when everything is going well
quiz.explication: “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7), giving in secret (Matthew 6:3-4).

quiz.q: What are the “firstfruits”?
choix: The leftovers of the harvest, given at the end
The first fruits, given to God first
quiz.explication: Giving first or giving the leftovers: these are two opposite theologies. Firstfruits say, “God is my priority and my security.”

quiz.q: What is the difference between the tithe and the offering?
choix: The tithe is the tenth given faithfully; the offering goes beyond it, from the heart
The tithe is voluntary, the offering mandatory
The tithe is for the poor, the offering for the church
quiz.explication: The tithe is the faithful foundation (the tenth); the freewill offering is added to it, as each one has purposed in his heart (2 Corinthians 9:7).

quiz.q: In practical terms, on an income of 1,500 euros, the tithe comes to…
quiz.explication: The tithe is one tenth: 150 euros out of 1,500. The principle is proportional: everyone is asked to take the same step of trust, whatever their income.

quiz.q: Why can we say that giving your money means giving part of your life?
choix: Because money is sacred in itself
Because money represents crystallized hours of life and work
Because you can't live without money
quiz.explication: Those hours of work turned into numbers in an account are life given. “For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:21).

quiz.q: In the Old Testament, what was the tithe used for, among other things?
choix: To support the Levites, set apart for God's service, and to sustain worship
quiz.explication: The tithe supported the Levites and worship; when it lapsed, God's servants abandoned their ministry and idolatry took hold (2 Chronicles 29:9).
